drills.q: When would you choose gRPC over REST for a new internal service, and what does it cost you operationally?
drills.a: Choose gRPC when both ends are yours, latency/payload size matter (Protobuf ~2-5x smaller than JSON), you want generated typed clients, and you need native streaming. Cost: no browser support without gRPC-Web/a proxy, needs HTTP/2-aware load balancers, harder to debug with curl (need grpcurl).

drills.q: Explain GraphQL over-fetching and under-fetching with concrete examples.
drills.a: Over-fetching: GET /users/1 returns all 50 fields when the client needed 2. Under-fetching: rendering one screen needs 3 sequential REST calls (user, then posts, then comment counts). GraphQL's single query with field selection fixes both, at the cost of URL-based cacheability and backend N+1 risk.

drills.q: Explain the GraphQL N+1 problem and how DataLoader fixes it. Does DataLoader fix N+1 across separate HTTP requests?
drills.a: A query resolving 20 users' posts fires 20+1 queries naively. DataLoader batches all requests for the same field issued within one event-loop tick into one WHERE user_id IN (...) query, and caches per request. It does NOT fix N+1 across separate requests -- its cache is scoped to one request/tick by design, since sharing it across requests would leak data between users.

drills.q: How do you stop a GraphQL API being used for denial-of-service via a pathological query, and why is depth limiting alone insufficient?
drills.a: Depth limiting (reject nesting past ~5-10 levels) plus cost/complexity analysis (per-field cost scaled by list-size args, reject over a budget). Depth limiting alone misses a SHALLOW query requesting a huge list (first: 100000) -- that's a breadth problem, which only cost analysis catches.

drills.q: WebSocket or SSE for a live stock ticker? What changes your answer?
drills.a: SSE -- client only receives, gets automatic reconnect via EventSource, works through existing HTTP infra. Changes to WebSocket if the client also needs to place a cancel order on the same low-latency channel mid-stream -- that's genuinely bidirectional.

drills.q: Design a webhook receiver safe against retries and out-of-order delivery.
drills.a: Verify HMAC signature on raw body before parsing. Atomic INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING keyed on provider event ID before acting (idempotent against retries). Check a sequence number/monotonic field per entity to reject/queue stale out-of-order events -- not wall-clock timestamps alone, since those can have skew.

drills.q: Polling vs long-polling vs webhook -- when is each the right call? What if the client is behind a NAT with no inbound access?
drills.a: Polling: simplest, tolerates latency up to interval. Long-polling: server holds request ~20-30s, better latency, ties up connections. Webhook: lowest latency, but needs a reachable inbound endpoint and you own reliability. Behind NAT with no inbound access, webhooks are off the table -- fall back to polling/long-polling.

drills.q: Why is a message queue sometimes the right answer to 'which protocol should I use'? When does it fail?
drills.a: It decouples producer/consumer lifetimes, buffers against downstream outages, and gives at-least-once delivery with replay (Kafka retains days of messages). It fails when the caller needs a synchronous answer now -- a queue just relocates the wait via a request/reply pattern (correlation ID + reply topic), which reintroduces most of what a direct call gave for free plus queue overhead.

drills.q: A team put GraphQL in front of a public, read-heavy, rarely-changing product catalog. What's wrong, and what would you do instead?
drills.a: They gave up CDN-level caching (every request is an uncacheable POST) for flexibility a static catalog browse page doesn't need. A REST endpoint with ?fields= plus Cache-Control/ETag gets most of the benefit with free CDN caching and none of the N+1/DoS surface. If mobile genuinely needs multi-screen assembly, use a BFF or persisted GraphQL queries (allow-listed, turned back into cacheable GETs) -- not an open public query surface.

drills.q: Compare cache-key composition risk across REST and GraphQL, and diagnose: a user reports seeing another user's personalized data from a shared CDN cache.
drills.a: REST keys naturally on URL; ignoring a query param (locale) serves wrong content. GraphQL has no default cache key at all (POST body) unless using persisted queries. The reported bug is a classic CDN misconfiguration: an auth-dependent/personalized field got cached at a shared (non-private) layer -- fix is Cache-Control: private on personalized responses or fetching personalization client-side, not just a key issue.

drills.q: Why do gRPC deadlines solve a problem plain HTTP timeouts don't, and does that mean gRPC automatically solves cancellation propagation too?
drills.a: gRPC deadlines propagate as wire metadata through the call chain -- each downstream hop sees the remaining budget, not a fresh timeout, unlike HTTP where each hop's timeout is independent unless manually threaded. It does NOT automatically solve cancellation -- a deadline expiring triggers cancellation on the gRPC context only if every hop actually checks the context at its await/blocking points; a service ignoring it keeps working past the deadline regardless.

drills.q: A downstream service occasionally takes 30+ seconds under load. Does that change your protocol choice, or is it a resilience problem?
drills.a: It's a resilience problem (timeout/retry/circuit breaker/bulkhead), not fixed by protocol choice alone. But if the caller doesn't actually need the result synchronously, that's the signal to move the call behind a queue: accept fast, return 202, process at the consumer's own pace -- converting a latency fight into a throughput problem. If the caller DOES need the result to render a page, a queue just relocates the wait.
